title: Earl Hines as her idol on the radio and Nat Cole's resemblance to him
summary: She listened to Hines from the Grand Terrace on a neighbor's radio, recalls Ray Nance and Walter Fuller, and says Nat Cole at the piano sounded like Hines before he began to sing.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Uh-huh.
And of course -- I don't know if I mentioned this in my early part of the interview either, where Hines was my idol. Did I mention that?
No, you didn't mention that.

I didn't? Oh, my aching tonsils, how could I forget that. Well, you know, Pat, years ago -- well, I'd say when I was in Louisiana. I'm going back to that now. My folks, well, we didn't have -- we didn't even have electricity, you know, and we used to go over to my neighbor's, our neighbor's, who lived across the street. Well, they had a very lovely home and they had, you know, a nice radio and everything, where we could go and listen to Hines and everybody. We didn't have

this at home. All we had was an old gramophone and played records, you know. But we would go over to my neighbor's and listen to Hines, who at that time was working the Grand Terrace in Chicago. And this was broadcast, used to come over the works, and it would come to Lake Charles. And we would stay up at night and listen to this. We'd go and listen. I think they were on every night, at least five nights a week or something like that, from the Grand Terrace, which was a beautiful, wonderful thing. And I was so -- well, I was just so thrilled over him. I just loved his work and still do. And he's the one guy who has, through the years -- and he looks so well today. He looks just marvelous.
He could play up a breeze and a storm, and then it comes back to my mind I used to hear Ray, Ray Nance was with that band at that time, when they played the Grand --
You heard Ray on the radio.
Oh, yes. He was -- oh, yes, with his violin. I could hear him play. He played violin at that time, I think, more than he played trumpet, with Hines. You know?
Uh-huh.
I don't think he played too much violin with Duke. You would know better about that than I would.
Well, he always played some. Like every night he would play violin, but not -- he played much more trumpet than he did violin. Trumpet and vocals more than
violin, I think.
Yeah.
But I don't think they ever did a performance where his violin wasn't included.

Well, he was playing the violin. This stuck out in my mind, you know, with Ray, with Hines, when they played the Grand Terrace, and I think Walter was with the band at that time, Walter Fuller. I think Fuller was with Hines at that particular time also. But anyway, I -- you know, this was one of the -- he was one of the guys who really, really, really did impress me. I was so thrilled and impressed with his style, you know. And Nat, getting back to Nat King Cole, when I heard Nat, Nat reminded me so very much of Hines., you know. You could tell he was greatly influenced by Hines And he just played so doggone much piano. I didn't ever bother about his singing, about him singing at that time. But later on the same thing that happened to him -- that happened to me, rather, happened to him, because it happened to him first, you know. And people started asking him to sing, and he kept saying, 'Well, I'm not -- you know, I don't sing.' And they insisted that he did sing, and then thank God they did, because he turned out to be a very fine, distinctive singer.
Yeah.
You know?
Yeah. I enjoyed it.
So that was one of the -- one of the things that stuck out in my mind, too. I was just very glad that I had known him before any of this ever happened.
Uh-huh.
